title: Cadence × Helix Health — Quarterly Business Review

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Good morning, everyone-thanks for joining the Q1 business review. I'm Alex Rivera, head of growth at Cadence, and I'll be hosting today.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Sarah Chen, solutions engineer, Cadence. Happy to be here and ready to dive into the data.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Nadia Hassan, CEO, Cadence. Looking forward to a productive session.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Elena Vasquez, VP of product at Helix Health. Thanks for having us.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Marcus Webb, VP of engineering, Helix Health. I’ll be keeping an eye on the technical bits.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Priya Raman, director of analytics, Helix Health. I’ll chime in on the dashboards we’ve built together.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: James Mbeki, CFO, Cadence. I’ll be on the call for the financial overview and contract side.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Tom Bradley, backend engineer, Cadence. I’ll step in if we need to get into any API or integration details.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Great, thanks all. Just to set the agenda: we’ll start with a quick roll-call, then I’ll walk through adoption numbers-seats up, weekly active a touch down. Elena will challenge the active metric definition, Sarah will clarify, we’ll address the August outage and the missed Epic integration, then Priya will share the readmission-risk dashboard impact, Tom will explain the technical slip, and we’ll close with next steps and renewal outlook. Any additions?

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: That covers it from our side, Alex. Maybe we should carve out a few minutes for the cohort-builder performance issue?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Good point, Elena. We’ll slot that in after the integration discussion. If there’s nothing else, let’s kick off with the adoption numbers.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Alright, let’s dive into the numbers. As of the end of Q1 we’ve got 1,842 active seats on the Cadence platform for Helix, up from 1,690 last quarter - that’s roughly a 9% increase, driven mostly by the new tele-triage modules we rolled out in February.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Nine percent is solid, thanks for that. Do you have a breakdown by role? I’m curious how many of those are clinicians versus admin.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sure thing. Clinicians are at 1,210 seats, up 12% quarter-over-quarter, while admin and support staff make up the remaining 632 - that’s a 4% rise, mostly from the scheduling desk expansion in the Midwest clinics.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Just to add, the new role-based access controls we introduced in early February helped us onboard those admin users faster, so the lag time from request to activation dropped from an average of 7 days to just 2 days.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Exactly, and that ties into the weekly active metric - which is where we see a slight dip. Weekly active users fell from 1,543 last quarter to 1,492 this quarter, about a 3.3% decrease.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Wait, is that 1,492 unique users per week, or does it count multiple logins?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Good question. It’s unique user count - we defined weekly active as any distinct user who logged in at least once during the week, regardless of how many times they accessed the system.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So the definition changed from the last QBR where we counted sessions instead of unique users?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Yeah, we adjusted the definition in March to align with our product analytics team’s standard KPI, which focuses on unique engagement rather than raw session volume. That’s why the number looks lower even though overall usage time actually went up by about 5%.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a financial perspective, the seat growth is what matters for the renewal calculations, but I’ll need the exact per-seat revenue uplift - can you pull the $ per seat figure for me?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sure, the average revenue per seat for Helix this quarter was $1,250 annually, up from $1,180 last quarter after the price adjustment we made in January.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Just to flag, the backend logs show a spike in API calls from the new tele-triage feature, which could be contributing to the higher usage time despite the dip in unique weekly actives.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Right, so to summarize: seats up 9%, clinician seats up 12%, admin seats up 4%; weekly active users down 3.3% due to a definition change, but total engagement minutes are up 5%, and per-seat revenue is now $1,250. Anything else before we move on?

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: No, that’s clear. Let’s keep going.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Hold on a second, Alex-this weekly active dip, you said it’s down 3.3%, but I’m not convinced that’s the whole story. How exactly are you defining ‘weekly active’ here? Because last quarter we were tracking sessions, not users, and that seemed to line up better with our clinical workflow reporting.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Right, so the metric we’re using now is unique users-any distinct user that logs in at least once during the week, regardless of how many times they actually open the app. We switched to that in March to match the product analytics standard.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Okay, unique users, got it. But does that include people who just pop in for a single glance, like a nurse checking a lab result and then logging out, or does it count only those who actually engage with a patient-facing module?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: It’s purely login-based. As soon as the auth token is generated, the user is counted for that week. We don’t have a minimum activity threshold built into the weekly active KPI yet.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So a one-off login could inflate the number, but then we’re seeing a dip-does that mean fewer people are even logging in once a week?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: That’s the paradox. Because we changed the definition, the raw count actually dropped even though overall session volume went up. In Q4 we had about 2,100 session counts per week, but those were spread over fewer unique users.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Hmm. And the session count you’re referencing-are those all API calls, or actual UI interactions? I need to know because our compliance team wants to see true clinical touchpoints, not background syncs.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: The session metric includes any authenticated interaction, so it captures UI page loads and also background data pulls like the vitals sync. We can break it down if you need a clean split between clinician-initiated actions and system-initiated calls.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Please do that. Also, can you pull the week-over-week trend for unique logins versus total sessions for the past 12 weeks? I want to see if there’s a pattern where the definition shift is masking a real usage decline.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sure thing, I’ll have the analytics dashboard export sent to you by end of day. And I’ll add a note to the next QBR deck clarifying the definition change so we’re all on the same page moving forward.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Sure, let me walk through exactly what we mean by ‘weekly active’-we’re counting any distinct user ID that authenticates at least once between Monday 00:00 UTC and Sunday 23:59 UTC. It doesn’t matter if they open a single chart, click a single button, or just hit the landing page; the moment the token is minted, we flag them as active for that week.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Okay, that’s clear, but you just said the previous quarter we were using sessions. Did we actually switch the definition in March, or was that a reporting error?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Good point, Elena. We did a formal change in March 2024, but the QBR deck we sent you in early February still referenced the old session-based metric. I’m sorry about that-our product analytics team rolled out the new definition in the back-end, but we missed updating the deck.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Yeah, I noticed that too when I was prepping the slides. I think the slide titled ‘Weekly Active Users’ still had the session count line from Q3.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Exactly. The session-based KPI counted any API call that resulted in a UI load, which inflated the numbers because background syncs were included. When we moved to unique-login counts, we stripped out those system-initiated calls, which is why the headline looks lower even though total engagement minutes are up.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So the dip we’re seeing isn’t a real usage drop, it’s just a metric shift?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: That’s right, but there’s a nuance: because we now count any login, even a nurse who just checks a lab result once a week gets counted, whereas before we required a minimum of two page loads to be considered active. So the new metric is actually more inclusive of low-touch users, which means the dip suggests we’re seeing fewer low-touch logins, not necessarily fewer high-touch interactions.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: If I may jump in-does the new definition affect any of the SLA reporting we do for uptime?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: It does, indirectly. Our SLA dashboards still pull from the same health-check endpoints, but the user-count layer is separate. I can export a side-by-side comparison showing the March-to-present unique-login numbers versus the Q3 session counts, so you can see the exact delta.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Please do. And can you also annotate the QBR deck with a footnote that says ‘Definition changed March 2024; prior quarters used session-based active metric’?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Absolutely. I’ll update the deck right after this call, push the revised version to the shared folder, and send a quick email summarizing the change. I’ll also include a CSV with the raw counts for the past 16 weeks so you can slice it any way you need.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Thanks, Sarah. That should clear up the confusion for the compliance folks and give us a solid baseline for next quarter’s reporting.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Look, I’ll be straight with you all-this reporting inconsistency is on us, and I take full responsibility for the mix-up.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Alex, we need specifics. How did the deck get out with the old metric after we’d already changed it?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: We rolled the backend change in early March, but the slide deck was finalized by the product marketing lead on Feb 27, and the update never made it back into the master file before the QBR prep started.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Right, the data pipeline was updated on March 3, but the deck version we used was still the February 24 copy.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: So essentially the finance team was looking at the wrong numbers for the whole quarter?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Exactly. When I pulled the numbers for the deck, I was looking at the live dashboard, which already reflected the new definition, but the static slide still had the old session-based line because I didn’t double-check the source file.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: That’s a pretty big oversight. It’s not just a typo; it changes how we interpret usage trends.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I get that, and I’m sorry. I’ve already set up a new review gate: any metric change triggers a mandatory cross-team sign-off before any deck is locked. That way the product, analytics, and finance leads will all sign a quick checklist.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Will that also include a version-control log so we can see who approved what and when?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Yes, we’re moving the deck to a SharePoint library with version history and required approvals. I’ll also add a footnote on every KPI slide that references the change log, so anyone opening the file can instantly see the definition date.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: And for this quarter’s audit, can you send us the revised deck plus the side-by-side CSV you mentioned, so we can re-run the compliance checks?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Absolutely, I’ll have the updated deck, the CSV, and a one-page summary of the change process in your inbox by 4 pm today. I’ll also schedule a brief follow-up with the compliance team tomorrow to walk through it.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Thanks, Alex. That should help us close the loop and keep the next QBR clean.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Appreciate the ownership, Alex. Let’s make sure this becomes the new norm, not a one-off fix.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Okay, I’ll jump in-our analytics team has actually shipped three major features on Cadence this quarter, plus a handful of smaller tweaks that I’ll skim over.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Three? I thought we were waiting on two?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Right, so the first is the cohort builder 2.0, which now supports multi-dimensional filters and can handle up to 10 million patients without timing out; we rolled that out on April 12 after a two-week beta with Helix’s research team.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: I remember that-there were a few edge-case bugs with the date-range picker that you guys patched on the fly.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Exactly, we pushed a hot-fix on April 19 that fixed the off-by-one error when the start date was the first of the month, and we added automated regression tests for all date-logic paths.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: And the second feature?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: The readmission-risk dashboard you saw in the demo-built on top of our new risk-score model that ingests discharge summaries, lab results, and social determinants data. That went live on May 5, and we’ve already seen a 12% reduction in 30-day readmission rates across the pilot hospitals, according to the preliminary analysis we sent you on May 22.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Those are the numbers we’re excited about, but I need to know the confidence interval on that 12% figure.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: We ran a bootstrapped sample of 4,000 discharges, 95% CI = 8.3% to 15.7%, so it’s statistically significant. The full methodology is in the appendix of the report I shared on the drive.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And the third?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: The compliance audit trail view-essentially a UI overlay that surfaces every data-access event for a given patient record, with timestamps, user IDs, and IP addresses. That was a request from your security team in March, and we delivered the MVP on June 1, then added role-based filtering on June 18 after your feedback that the initial view was too noisy.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: That ties into our financial reporting requirements, so good to have that baked in.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: One more quick note: we also released a set of 15 new API endpoints for custom metric extraction, and we documented them in Swagger on June 25, which should help your data-science pipelines avoid the old work-arounds you were using.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Great, that’s a lot more than I was expecting. Can you send a consolidated release notes doc?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Absolutely-I'll email a PDF that consolidates all four releases, the performance benchmarks, and the open tickets list by end of day. And I’ll schedule a 30-minute walkthrough for any team that wants a deeper dive.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: The readmission-risk dashboard we rolled out on May 5 basically gives your clinicians a real-time risk score for each patient right after discharge, pulling in the latest lab values, discharge notes, and even zip-code level social determinant indices.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So instead of waiting for the nightly batch, they see a flag on the patient’s chart within minutes?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Exactly. In the pilot at three of your hospitals-St. Mark’s, Riverside, and Greenfield-we saw that physicians started intervening on high-risk patients an average of 2.3 hours earlier than they would have otherwise.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And the UI lets them drill down - click the risk meter, see the top three contributing factors, like elevated BUN, recent ICU stay, or lack of follow-up appointments.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: We noticed the alert volume was manageable too - about 8 alerts per 100 discharges, which is low enough not to cause alert fatigue.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: What kind of interventions are we talking about? Discharge planning? Home health referrals?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Both. In Riverside, for example, the care-coordination team added a home-visit nurse for 57% of the flagged patients, and that correlated with a 14% drop in 30-day readmissions compared with the prior month.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: That’s impressive. Did you also see any change in length-of-stay?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: A modest effect - the average LOS for flagged patients dropped from 4.2 days to 3.9 days, which translates to roughly 120 bed-days saved across the three sites in the first six weeks.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a financial perspective, that’s about $1.1 million in avoided costs, assuming $9,200 per readmission, not to mention the penalty avoidance under the HRRP.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Do we have any qualitative feedback from the clinicians?

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Yes - the chief of medicine at St. Mark’s told us the dashboard gave them confidence to justify early follow-up appointments, and the nursing staff said the risk breakdown helped them prioritize discharge education.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: We also built a quick export button so they can pull the risk cohort into your existing care-management platform, which some teams have already started using for targeted outreach.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Overall, the early data suggest a statistically significant 12% reduction in 30-day readmissions with a 95% confidence interval of 8.3% to 15.7%, and the clinical staff are reporting higher satisfaction with the decision-support tool.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Before we go any further, I need to bring up the August outage - it was four hours right in the middle of our month-end close, and it really threw a wrench in the reconciliation process.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Right, I remember the timing was terrible. Can you walk us through exactly what happened and what impact it had on your reporting?

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Sure. At 2:15 PM on August 12, the Cadence API gateway went down, and because we pull transaction logs in real time for our financial close, the feed stopped. Our finance team couldn’t finalize the daily revenue figures for August 12-13, which meant the month-end close was delayed by a full business day.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I’m really sorry to hear that. Our post-mortem showed it was a misconfiguration in the load balancer after a routine patch. We should have caught that earlier.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: I get that, but the downstream effect was that we missed the deadline for filing the internal audit report on August 20, and we had to push the external audit to September 5, which is now cutting into our next reporting cycle.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Just to add, the outage also caused a cascade failure in the batch export jobs that feed the cohort builder - those jobs were stuck in a retry loop for about two hours before they finally gave up.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Exactly, and because the cohort builder was down, our analytics team couldn’t generate the variance analysis they needed for the month-end variance reconciliation, so they ended up doing a manual extract from the database, which is both error-prone and time-consuming.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a contractual standpoint, the SLA for uptime is 99.9%, which translates to about 7.2 hours of downtime per month. Four hours is within that window, but the timing during month-end is a material breach of our service expectations.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: I’m not just talking about the raw downtime - it’s the fact that the outage hit us during a critical reporting window, forced us to re-run multiple ETL pipelines, and ultimately cost us roughly 120 engineer-hours to clean up the data gaps and re-issue the reports.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Understood. We need to figure out how to prevent this happening again, especially during any future close periods. Let’s dive into the root cause and see what mitigation steps we can put in place.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Okay, let me take this straight from the top because I feel this really reflects on us, not just on the platform.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: On August 12 at 14:12 UTC we pushed a routine security patch to the load balancer that sits in front of our API gateway. The patch itself was clean, but the config we applied unintentionally disabled the health-check endpoint for the primary node.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Our monitoring system saw the health-check failures and, thinking the node was down, automatically routed all traffic to the secondary node, which at that moment was already at 95% CPU from the previous day's batch jobs.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Within two minutes the secondary node hit a throttling limit, the gateway started returning 502 errors, and the auto-scale policy didn’t fire because the load balancer thought the primary was simply offline, not that we needed more capacity.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We didn’t get an alert until the API latency spiked past our 2-second threshold at 14:18, and by then the finance ETL pipeline had already timed out and started queuing retries.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: The root cause was a missing ‘allow-health-check-override’ flag in the patch script - something our DevOps checklist omitted because the previous patch a month earlier had the flag set to true and we assumed it persisted.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I’ve personally taken responsibility for that oversight; I signed off on the change request and didn’t double-check the diff before merging.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: To be transparent, the post-mortem shows three immediate impacts: the four-hour API outage you described, the cascade failure in the cohort-builder batch jobs that Tom mentioned, and the downstream manual effort you quantified at roughly 120 engineer-hours.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We also saw a secondary impact on the real-time dashboards used by your clinical ops team - they showed a sudden drop to zero active users for about 30 minutes, which I know caused alarm on your end-user side.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Going forward, we’ve instituted three concrete changes: first, a mandatory peer-review of any load-balancer config change that includes a health-check validation step; second, an updated alerting rule that fires on any health-check failure longer than 30 seconds, not just latency; third, a rollback script that automatically restores the previous config within five minutes if the new config disables health checks.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We’ve already run a tabletop drill with the engineering team this afternoon to validate the new rollback, and the run-book is now version 2.1 in our internal wiki.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I know this outage hit you at the worst possible time, and I’m sorry for the operational pain it caused. I’m personally overseeing the implementation of these mitigations and will provide you with a weekly status report for the next six weeks.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Nadia, I appreciate the detail, but the bottom line for us is the SLA breach - we were promised 99.9% uptime, and this four-hour window knocked us well below that, so we need to discuss the credit we’re owed under the contract.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I hear you, Marcus, and I’m not trying to dodge the SLA language - the clause does allow for service credits when uptime falls below the threshold, but we have to calculate the exact percentage for the month.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Exactly, and we’ve run the numbers on our side - for August we’re looking at 96.2% overall availability, which translates to a 3.8% shortfall. That should trigger a 15% credit on the monthly bill, per section 4.2.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Just to jump in, the contract does say a 10% credit for any month under 99.5%, and an additional 5% if the outage exceeds two hours, so the total would be 15% as you’re indicating, Marcus.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Right, but we also have the clause about "critical reporting windows" where an outage beyond 30 minutes incurs a double-penalty credit. That’s not just a standard SLA - it’s a specific addendum we signed last year.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I’m aware of that addendum, and I’m not disputing the entitlement - my question is how we apply it retroactively, given the outage was on the 12th and the billing cycle closed on the 31st.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: We can prorate the credit based on the days impacted. If we take the 4-hour outage and apply the double-penalty multiplier, the credit comes out to roughly 18% of the August invoice, which is what we’d be prepared to issue.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: That’s more in line with what we need, but we also have to consider the downstream cost - the 120 engineer-hours you mentioned translates to about $24,000 in direct labor for us, plus the delayed reporting that affected our quarterly close.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Understood, Marcus. While the SLA credit covers the service downtime, we can discuss a one-time goodwill adjustment to offset part of those labor costs, perhaps a $10,000 credit on top of the SLA-based percentage.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: If we can agree on the 18% SLA credit plus a $10,000 goodwill adjustment, that would bring us close to a fair resolution and let us move forward without escalating the issue to legal.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: I’ll need to get final approval from finance, but I’m confident we can sign off on that combined package by end of day tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Great, I’ll have my team draft the amendment and send it over for signatures. Let’s also set a brief follow-up call Friday to confirm the credit is reflected in the next invoice.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Alright, let me lay out exactly what the contract says so we’re all on the same page - Section 4.2 spells out the base SLA credit of 10% for any month where the weighted uptime falls below 99.5%.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Then, per the addendum we signed in March 2023, there’s an extra 5% kicker if the outage exceeds two consecutive hours, which is why you’ve been hearing the 15% figure.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: What’s less obvious, though, is the "critical reporting window" clause - that’s in Exhibit B, paragraph 3 - it triggers a double-penalty credit, meaning the base 10% becomes 20% for that month, and the extra 5% also doubles to 10%, so you’re looking at a potential 30% credit if we applied it strictly.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: We’ve run the math both ways with our legal team; the most defensible position, given the outage was 4 hours but split across two windows, is the 18% figure you quoted, which is the 10% base plus the 5% two-hour add-on, then multiplied by 1.5 because the outage hit a reporting window.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: That 1.5 multiplier brings us to roughly 22.5% of the August invoice - but we’re willing to round it to 20% as a goodwill gesture, because we recognize the impact on your month-end close.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Beyond the pure contract language, Cadence wants to do more than just the credit. We’ll also allocate a dedicated engineering sprint next quarter to harden the rollback process you mentioned, and we’ll provide a quarterly health-check report that includes the latency metrics for the cohort builder you flagged earlier.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: In addition, we’ll give you a $5,000 voucher for any of our premium add-ons - the predictive analytics module or the custom API connectors - that you might want to trial before the next renewal cycle.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: To make sure this isn’t just talk, I’ll have our finance ops team send a formal amendment by COB tomorrow, and I’ll copy you, Nadia, and Marcus so you can see the exact language and the credit calculation worksheet attached.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Finally, I propose a short-term SLA dashboard be shared with your team starting next Monday, so you can monitor uptime in real time and we can flag any deviation before it turns into a breach. That’s the extra step we’re adding beyond the contract to rebuild trust.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Okay, before we move on, I need to bring up the Epic integration - we were promised delivery in Q3, but we still haven’t seen a production-ready endpoint.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Right, the integration. I’ll be straight - we missed the original target because the new FHIR-to-REST mapping layer hit an unexpected dependency on the patient-identity service that wasn’t stabilized until early September.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Early September? That’s basically the start of Q4. We were counting on that to feed the readmission-risk dashboard with real-time Epic data for the fall cohort.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: I get that, and it’s on us. The thing is, the dependency was introduced in the 2.4.1 release, and we only got the final API spec from Epic on August 22, which forced us to rewrite the transformation logic on the fly.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: So you’re saying the spec change was after the deadline? That’s a big shift for us, because we’ve already built out the UI widgets that expect the data shape from the original spec.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Exactly. And the rewrite added about 3,200 lines of code, plus a new integration test suite that we had to spin up. We’ve now got it in our staging environment, but we still need another sprint to do the end-to-end performance validation - especially the 200 TPS throughput that Helix expects during peak admission spikes.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: 200 TPS is non-negotiable for us. If the integration can’t handle that, our clinicians will see lag, and the whole clinical decision-support story falls apart. We’ve already pushed back the internal rollout to November 15 because of this delay.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We’re targeting a hard go-live on November 30. That gives us three weeks to finish load testing, address any bottlenecks, and get the security review signed off. I’ll personally own the final validation sprint and keep you in the loop daily.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: November 30 is cutting it close, but if you can guarantee the 200 TPS benchmark and the data mapping matches the Epic v2024-09 schema, we can adjust our internal timeline. I need a concrete confidence level - are we looking at 80% confidence or higher?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Based on the latest test runs, we’re at 92% confidence for the throughput, and the data mapping validation has a 98% pass rate. I’ll send you the detailed test report by tomorrow EOD, and we can set up a joint review call on Thursday at 10 am PST to walk through the numbers.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Alright, that works. Just make sure the report includes the latency breakdown per endpoint and the error-rate thresholds we discussed last month. If anything looks off, we’ll need to re-negotiate the go-live date.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Understood. I’ll also add a risk-mitigation checklist to the deliverable - things like fallback to batch sync if the real-time stream drops below 150 TPS for more than five minutes.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Good. Let’s lock that in. We’ll update our roadmap slide for the next executive review and note the November 30 target with the 92% confidence flag.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Look, the core issue was that the FHIR-to-REST mapping layer we built for the Epic bridge depends on the patient-identity microservice, and that service was still in beta when we cut the Q3 deadline.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Beta? You mean it wasn’t even GA?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Exactly, it was running a feature flag that only flipped on September 5 after we got the final spec, so the mapper kept hitting a 404 on every patient lookup.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: And you kept pushing that downstream?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We didn’t have a choice - the mapper was hard-wired to the identity endpoint’s response schema, which changed from the draft v1.2 to the final v1.3. That forced us to rewrite the transformation logic for every resource type, not just Encounter but also Observation and Condition.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So the spec change was the root?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Yes, the Epic team released the v2024-09 schema on August 22, three weeks after our internal cutoff. That meant we had to retro-fit 3,200 new lines of code, add a new validation framework, and regenerate the OpenAPI contracts for each endpoint.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Did you at least have unit coverage?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We started with about 45% coverage in the 2.4.1 release, but after the rewrite we pushed it up to 87% using the new test harness. The integration test suite also grew from 120 to 380 test cases, many of which simulate the high-volume admission spikes you mentioned.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: What about the performance bottleneck?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: The bottleneck turned out to be the synchronous patient-identity lookup during the transformation pipeline. Each lookup added roughly 12 ms latency, which multiplied across the 200 TPS target. To fix it we introduced a caching layer with a 5-minute TTL and refactored the mapper to batch requests in groups of 50, cutting the per-record latency to about 4 ms.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: And the security review?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Because the new cache touches PHI, we had to get a separate SOC-2 addendum signed. That added another two weeks of compliance work, but the security team cleared it on November 12, so we’re now only three weeks out from the go-live target.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Alright, so the slip is purely a cascade of dependency timing, spec change, and compliance overhead?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: That’s the technical chain, yes - no excuses, just facts. We’ve documented every change in the Jira epic EPIC-INT-342, and the burn-down chart shows we’re back on track for the November 30 hard deadline with the confidence numbers I shared earlier.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Look, I’m really feeling the pressure here-this delay isn’t just a line item on a spreadsheet, it’s directly pulling the rug out from under the predictive-analytics module we promised to have in production by early December.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Elena, I hear you, but the outage and the integration slip are two separate beasts; we can’t magically accelerate one because the other stalled.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: That’s exactly the point, Marcus-our roadmap is a single chain. The readmission-risk dashboard we launched in October was supposed to feed into the new care-pathway engine that launches in Q1, and now that engine is missing its patient-identity feed because of the Epic lag.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We’ve added a fallback cache as a stop-gap, but it does mean the downstream risk scores are slightly less granular until the full schema sync happens.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: A stop-gap is fine for internal testing, but our clinical ops team has already booked training sessions for January 15, and they’re counting on the full fidelity data. If we can’t deliver that, we’ll have to push those trainings back, which cascades into staffing and budget approvals.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Elena, I get the frustration-our post-mortem on the outage already showed we need tighter release gates, but the integration timeline was set by the Epic team’s own release calendar, which we didn’t control.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Control or not, Cadence sold us a guarantee that the integration would be live by Q3. The contract language on ‘delivery milestones’ is pretty clear, and we’re now looking at a three-month slip that throws off our own Q4 product launch for the new tele-monitoring suite.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: We’ve reviewed the SLA language, and while the outage credits are straightforward, the integration delay falls under the ‘force-majeure’ clause because the schema change was a third-party release. That said, we’re willing to discuss a goodwill credit to offset the operational impact you’re describing.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: A goodwill credit doesn’t fix the fact that our clinicians will be using an incomplete view of patient history during the pilot, and that could affect outcomes metrics we need for the upcoming CMS reporting cycle.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: If it helps, we can prioritize a hot-fix that pushes the latest schema sync into the next sprint-maybe we can shave a week off the November 30 target if we allocate an extra engineer from the platform team.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: That would be a start, but I need a concrete commitment: a revised integration go-live date, a clear mitigation plan for the care-pathway engine, and a documented impact assessment for the tele-monitoring rollout. Otherwise, my leadership will have to re-prioritize the entire Q1 roadmap, which is not something we want to do.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Understood. I’ll put together a detailed risk-mitigation addendum by tomorrow, and we can schedule a follow-up with the Epic liaison early next week to lock down the final schema version. I’ll also flag the extra engineer resource with our PMO.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Okay, that’s better. Just make sure the addendum includes the exact latency numbers after the cache change, the revised test-coverage percentages, and a timeline that shows the new expected go-live on December 12 instead of November 30, so I can update our internal Gantt.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Okay, so let's lock this down-Elena, you asked for December 12 as the new go-live, correct?

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Yes, that's what we need to present to our steering committee tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We can commit to a hard deadline of December 12, but I have to be honest-the confidence level is about 70% given the remaining schema validation and the cache latency tuning still pending.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Seventy percent feels low for a critical integration. What would bump that up? Can we add another engineer or push a parallel stream?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: We can pull in a senior platform engineer from the Cloud team-Jenny Patel-who's free next week. That should get us to roughly 85% confidence, assuming no new Epic changes.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: 85% is better, but we still have to account for the training on Jan 15. If we slip again, we lose that window.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We can also add a contingency buffer: run a dry-run integration on December 5 with the fallback cache in place, then have a 48-hour window to fix any show-stopper before the official go-live.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a contractual standpoint, if we meet the December 12 date with that 85% confidence and the dry-run, we consider the SLA fulfilled. If we miss, we’ll trigger the goodwill credit we discussed earlier.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: The dry-run plan is doable. I’ll schedule it for December 5, allocate Jenny and another dev on Dec 6-8 for any fixes, and we’ll have a final sign-off meeting on December 10 with both teams.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Alright, that gives me something concrete to report. I’ll update the Gantt to show December 12 as the go-live with an 85% confidence rating and note the dry-run on the 5th as a mitigation step.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Great. To recap: revised go-live December 12, 85% confidence, dry-run Dec 5, extra engineer added, and we’ll deliver the risk-mitigation addendum by tomorrow. Any objections?

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: No objections, just a reminder to keep the Epic liaison looped in daily.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: I'll set up a shared channel for those updates and make sure the schema version is locked by Nov 28.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: And I'll have legal draft a brief amendment noting the new date and confidence level for the record.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Sounds good. We'll also note the goodwill credit trigger if we fall short of the 85% confidence threshold.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Thanks, everyone. I think we have a workable plan.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Before we get too deep into the integration timeline, I need to bring up the cohort builder performance issue we hit when we scaled up to 1.2 million active patients last month.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Right, that’s been on our radar. What’s the current latency?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: We’re seeing average query times of 14 seconds, spikes up to 45 seconds on complex filters, which is well above the sub-5-second SLA we promised for the Q2 release.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Those numbers are from the last dashboard export, right?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Exactly. The raw logs show the bottleneck is in the join operation between the patient-demographics table and the longitudinal-visits table. When the cohort size exceeds about 250 k records, the query planner falls back to a full table scan.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We knew the planner would behave that way, but we underestimated the growth curve after the new referral program launched in July.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: The referral program added roughly 400 k new patient records in two weeks, pushing us past the threshold. The result is that clinicians are waiting too long for the risk-stratification reports, and we’ve already gotten three tickets from the cardiology team complaining about timeout errors.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: That’s unacceptable, especially after the August outage. We need a fix before the December go-live, otherwise we’ll be back in the same blame game.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Our analytics team built a provisional materialized view that pre-aggregates the most common joins, which cuts the average latency to about 7 seconds, but it adds a nightly refresh cost and it’s not a long-term solution.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Can we automate that refresh more frequently? The nightly window is too coarse for real-time decision making.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: We’re experimenting with incremental refreshes every hour, but the current infrastructure can’t handle the write load without throttling other services. We’d need to provision an additional compute node in the Spark cluster, which would increase our cloud spend by roughly $12 k per month.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: That cost is not trivial, but if it prevents missed revenue from delayed cohort analyses, it may be justifiable. Do we have a business case?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Yes, the cardiology team estimates a $250 k revenue impact per month if they can’t access timely risk scores. The incremental refresh would recover most of that, so the ROI is strong.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: From a product roadmap perspective, we need a permanent fix-maybe re-architect the join strategy or move to a columnar store.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: Agreed. Our long-term plan is to migrate the cohort builder to a Snowflake-backed data mart, which would give us automatic clustering and better scaling. That migration is slated for Q3 2025, but we can fast-track a pilot for Helix by Q1 next year.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: In the meantime, can we at least raise the current confidence level for the cohort builder from 60% to 80% by adding that extra Spark node and enabling the hourly refresh?

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: If we allocate the node and adjust the job schedule, we can hit the 80% confidence target within a week. I’ll draft a short change request and send it over for approval.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Alright, let’s lock that in. Priya, you’ll own the node provisioning and the refresh schedule, and we’ll track the latency metrics daily. Any objections?

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: No objections, just make sure we document the cost impact for finance.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Okay, shifting gears-our engineering team has been working on a full rewrite of the query engine to address exactly the latency issues you just described, and we think a beta of that could be in a test environment by early November.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Right, the new engine swaps out the current row-based executor for a vectorized pipeline and adds adaptive query caching; in our internal benchmarks on a synthetic Helix-sized dataset we saw median query times drop from 7 seconds to about 2.3 seconds.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Two point three seconds sounds great, but can you walk us through what that means for our existing cohort builder jobs? Are we looking at a drop-in replacement or a migration effort?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: It’s not a drop-in today. The API surface is stable, but the underlying execution plan expects the new metadata schema. We’ve built a compatibility shim that can translate the old job definitions, but you’d still need to re-run the job compile step and validate the results against the current baseline.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So essentially we’d have to re-run our validation suite, which is a non-trivial effort given the 200+ cohort definitions we have. Can we get a sandbox where we can run that validation without touching production?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Yes, we can spin up a dedicated dev cluster with the beta engine. It would mirror your production data snapshot from last week, and you’d have full read/write access to test the migration scripts. We’ll also provide a migration toolkit that auto-generates the new job manifests.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I’m concerned about timelines-if we start testing in early November, when could we realistically go live without jeopardizing the December go-live for the other fixes?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: If the validation passes in about two weeks, we could schedule a phased rollout starting the first week of December. That would align with your existing maintenance window and give us a safety net before the end-of-year reporting freeze.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a financial perspective, an early access to the new engine could reduce the incremental compute cost we were talking about earlier. If we can cut latency to under three seconds, we might be able to drop the extra Spark node and still meet the 80% confidence SLA.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: That would be a win, but we need a guarantee that the rewrite won’t introduce regressions in edge cases-like the rare complex joins the cardiology team runs. Can we get a formal sign-off criteria?

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: We’ll draft a sign-off matrix that includes latency thresholds, result parity percentages, and error-rate caps. Once you approve the test plan, we’ll lock in the early-access schedule and get the sandbox ready by next Monday.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Alright, before we get too deep into the technical rollout, can we pivot to the contract renewal? We’re looking at a twelve-month extension, and I want to make sure we’re aligned on expectations.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sure thing, Elena. From our side, we’re happy to continue the partnership. We’ve drafted a renewal proposal that mirrors the current pricing, with a 3% uplift to account for the new features we’ll be delivering next year.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Just to add, the uplift is primarily for the advanced analytics modules and the upcoming clinical operations expansion we discussed earlier. It’s not a blanket increase.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From finance, a 3% increase is within our budget forecasts, but we need to see a detailed cost-benefit breakdown for the new modules, especially the ROI on the query engine rewrite and the cohort builder improvements.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: I hear that, James, but let me be blunt: the renewal will be scrutinised by our board next month. They’ll be looking at both the financials and the delivery track record, especially after the August outage and the integration delay.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Absolutely, and I take full responsibility for those hiccups. We’ve already put in place the SLA credit process we talked about, and the new engine rollout is on track to meet the December timeline, which should help restore confidence.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: If it helps, we can provide a performance audit report by the end of next week, showing the before-and-after metrics for latency, cost per query, and the projected savings over the next twelve months.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: That would be useful. Also, we need a clear roadmap for the Epic integration-still a Q4 deliverable, right? Any risk of further slip would be a red flag for renewal.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: We’ve re-baselined the Epic integration for early Q1 2025, with a built-in buffer. I can share the updated project plan and the risk mitigation steps we’ve added.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Okay, so to summarize: we need the audit report, the updated Epic integration timeline, and a revised financial justification for the 3% uplift. If those are solid, I can take the renewal package to the board with confidence.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Got it. I’ll have the audit ready by Friday, and Sarah will send the integration plan by tomorrow. James, I’ll get the cost-benefit spreadsheet over to you by end of day Thursday.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Perfect. I’ll review it and get back to you early next week so we can keep the renewal conversation moving.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Thanks, everyone. Let’s reconvene on this after the board review, say next Tuesday at 10 am? That should give us enough time to incorporate any feedback.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sounds good. I’ll put the invite out. Appreciate the candidness, Elena-let’s make sure this renewal is a win-win.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Okay, before we lock down the renewal, I want to pivot to something we’ve been flagging on our side for a while: getting Cadence deeper into the clinical operations workflow at Helix.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Sure, Nadia. What exactly are you envisioning?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We’ve got a dedicated Clinical Ops unit-about 12 physicians, 8 nurse managers, and a data-science liaison-who are still using a mix of spreadsheets and legacy tools for bed-turnover forecasting, staff scheduling, and discharge coordination. I’d like to see Cadence’s analytics layer plug into that, not just the readmission-risk dashboard.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: We’ve actually built a few of those connectors for other clients, like the real-time staffing optimizer we did for Mercy Health. It’s a matter of mapping your data sources and exposing the right APIs.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly, Sarah. What I need is a concrete commitment: a pilot that runs in the next 60 days, covering at least two of our high-volume units-ICU and Med-Surg. If we can demonstrate a 10-15% reduction in average length of stay or a 5% improvement in staff utilization, we’ll fast-track a full rollout.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: From a technical standpoint, we can spin up an isolated environment for the pilot within a week. We just need access to your Cerner feeds and the staffing roster exports; the rest is plug-and-play.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: I’ll add that we’ll need to tag the pilot data separately in our cohort builder so we can run pre-post analyses without contaminating the rest of your datasets.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: That’s fine, Priya. Also, can we lock in a dedicated success manager for this effort? We’ve had turnover on the Helix side, and I want a single point of contact to keep everything aligned.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Absolutely. I’ll have Sarah assign one of our senior solutions engineers-maybe Maya Patel-to be the day-to-day lead. She’ll sit in on your daily ops huddles and make sure the dashboards are feeding the right metrics.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: One more thing, Nadia: we need to agree on the success criteria up front. If we’re aiming for a 10-15% LOS reduction, we should define the baseline period, the patient mix, and the statistical confidence level-say 95%-so the board feels comfortable with the numbers.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Agreed. Let’s have Priya draft the measurement plan and send it over by Thursday. If we can sign off on the pilot scope by Friday, we’ll be ready to kick off on Monday the 2nd of next month. Does that timeline work for everyone?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: That works on our end. I’ll coordinate with the infrastructure team to provision the sandbox on Tuesday, so we have a day to validate the data pipelines before the pilot goes live.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Great. I’ll get the clinical ops leadership sign-off and loop them into the invite. Thanks, everyone-this is exactly the kind of expansion we need to keep the partnership moving forward.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Look, Nadia, I hear the ambition and I think there’s real value, but I can’t promise a full-scale rollout until we see the pilot data.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Understood, Elena-so you’d be okay with a limited engagement first?

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Exactly, a limited engagement. If the metrics hit the thresholds we discussed, we can fast-track the broader integration.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: That sounds like a reasonable gate. We could also set up a joint steering committee to review the results weekly.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: A steering committee would give us visibility, yes. I’d need representation from your analytics lead-maybe Priya-and from our product ops team.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: I can be on that, and I’ll make sure the cohort-builder tags are ready for the weekly sync.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Great. And just to be clear, the committee would have the authority to adjust scope or resources if we see early signals that the pilot is exceeding expectations.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: That flexibility is exactly what we need. It also helps our board feel comfortable with the investment.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: One more thing-I can’t lock in a permanent seat on the Helix side just yet, but I can earmark a senior product manager to shadow the pilot and start drafting a roadmap for the full Clinical Ops integration, assuming we hit the 10-15% LOS reduction.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: From the engineering side, that’s fine. We’ll make sure the API endpoints we expose are versioned so the roadmap can evolve without breaking the pilot.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: So, to sum up: we’ll proceed with the 60-day pilot, set up a weekly steering committee with Priya and a Cadence product lead, and I’ll assign a senior product manager to start a high-level integration plan that we can flesh out once we have the data.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: That’s perfect, Elena. Thanks for keeping the door open.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: My pleasure. Let’s reconvene after the first week of data to see if any tweaks are needed before we lock in the next phase.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Okay, let’s capture the action items so we all leave with the same list-I'll start: the pilot kickoff is set for September 11, 2024, and that's on me to coordinate the initial data feed from Helix into Cadence.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: I'll own the cohort-builder tag configuration and have the first batch of tags ready for the September 18 sync; that gives us a week to test the mapping against the pilot cohort.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: From engineering, I'll deliver the versioned API spec by September 15 and push the sandbox endpoint to production by September 20, so the pilot can start pulling real-time data without any breaking changes.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: I'll appoint a senior product manager-Sara Lopez-to shadow the pilot and draft the high-level integration roadmap; she'll have a draft version to share with you all by October 5.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: I need to make sure our monitoring dashboards are tuned for the pilot load; I'll have the alert thresholds defined and the dashboard view shared by September 22.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: On the finance side, I'll pull the revised SLA credit schedule and send the amendment to the contract by September 30, so we’re aligned before the next billing cycle.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I'll get the clinical ops leadership sign-off on the pilot charter and circulate the approved document to the steering committee by September 12, so we have board visibility early.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: I'll prepare the updated reporting definition-clearly stating weekly active users as unique logins per 7-day window-and distribute the revised deck to everyone by September 14, to avoid any more confusion.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: The weekly steering committee will meet every Monday at 10 AM Pacific; the first meeting is set for September 23, and I'll send calendar invites to Priya, Alex, and Tom right after this call.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Finally, I'll compile all these items into a single project plan, attach owners and due dates, and share the master doc in the Cadence-Helix shared folder by end of day tomorrow, September 6, so we can track progress in real time.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Alright, I think we’ve covered everything-thanks everyone for the energy today, especially given the tough spots we dug into.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Absolutely, Alex. I appreciate the candor, and I’m glad we could land on concrete next steps rather than just circling back later.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And hey, if we can keep the reporting definitions straight, maybe we’ll finally stop the weekly active confusion-my spreadsheet is already updating itself, promise.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Haha, good one, Sarah. On my end, I’ll make sure the finance folks don’t get any surprise credits after the fact-so you can all sleep easier.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Just a heads-up-once the monitoring dashboards are live, I’ll ping you all if I see any spikes during the pilot, especially if the August outage ghosts show up again.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Sounds good. And I’ll have that versioned API spec in the repo by the 15th, with the changelog so nobody gets blindsided.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Thanks, Tom. Also, I’ll add a quick note to the steering committee agenda about the upcoming in-person QBR-maybe we can finally swap the Zoom background for a real conference room.

turns.speaker: Priya Raman
turns.text: I’m all for that. I’ve already started scouting a few hotels in San Diego-perfect weather for a data-driven deep dive, and we can actually walk to lunch instead of ordering in.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: San Diego sounds amazing. If we can lock in a date, I’ll ask our clinical ops team to bring a few case studies to share in person-nothing like seeing the dashboards on a big screen.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Great, I’ll check the calendar and propose the first week of November; that should give us enough runway after the pilot wraps up.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And I’ll bring the updated deck printed-so we can flip pages instead of scrolling, which is a novelty for some of us!

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Just promise me there’ll be coffee; I’m not sure I can survive a whole day of spreadsheets without caffeine.

turns.speaker: Marcus Webb
turns.text: Coffee, snacks, and maybe a quick ping-pong break-let’s make that QBR a bit more fun than the usual marathon.

turns.speaker: Elena Vasquez
turns.text: Deal. And if anyone’s still skeptical about the pilot, we’ll have live data to show-nothing beats seeing the numbers in real time.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Alright, I’ll send out the meeting invite for the QBR once I hear back on the dates, and we’ll lock the venue. Thanks again, everyone-looking forward to seeing many of you in person soon!
